title: SkillSmith: Enhancing Locally Deployed Agents via Automatic Skill Construction and Evolution
prompt:

title: Physics-Informed Learning for Robust Acoustic Localization with Calibrated Uncertainty
prompt:
I've been developing an approach to physics-plausibility gating with a learned correction on top of a hyperbolic solver, aimed at bounding the catastrophic tail of localization errors without disturbing the cases where the solver is already reliable. The idea is to keep a TabPFN regression model that predicts source $x$ and $y$ coordinates independently, using 72 physics-informed tabular features per detection, with the hyperbolic solver's own position estimate included as one of the input features so the learned model is refining the physics-based solution rather than localizing from scratch. By default I retain the solver's estimate, and I only substitute the TabPFN prediction on detections flagged as unreliable by a two-stage plausibility gate. The first stage checks whether the solver's estimate falls within a bounding box around the microphone array, expanded outward by a tunable margin proportional to the array's spatial extent; anything outside is rejected unconditionally. The second stage, applied only to estimates surviving the first, computes an energy-consistency score as the RMS residual between each microphone pair's observed log-amplitude ratio and the ratio predicted from the candidate position under $1/r$ spherical spreading, and flags the estimate if this residual exceeds a threshold $\tau^*$. Since source loudness and microphone sensitivity cancel in the ratio, this check needs no absolute sound-level calibration; it's the amplitude-domain analogue of ratio-based energy localization, used here as a plausibility check rather than as a localizer itself. I select $\tau^*$ on simulation data alone, choosing the most permissive value by grid search that achieves at least a threefold improvement in 99th-percentile error for no more than a 20% increase in median error relative to the unsubstituted solver, then apply it unchanged to the field data with no tuning on field labels. A detection gets substituted with the TabPFN prediction if either the geometric check fails or the energy-consistency residual exceeds $\tau^*$; otherwise the solver's estimate is kept. My setup uses simulated multichannel acoustic experiments generated with the ForestIR package for the frozen-lake site, a low-noise, treeless site (so trunk scattering is disabled in simulation), with a bird-vocalization source placed at random 2D locations relative to a fixed three-microphone array in an approximately equilateral geometry with roughly 50 m inter-microphone spacing, microphones and speakers at 1.2 m height. Simulated weather is sampled from the range recorded during the real experiment (-19 to -6 degrees C, 70-95% RH), and each simulated recording draws one noise regime at random from the site's own recorded background, synthetic white, or pink noise, each at a fixed level. I also have real playback recordings from the Konnevesi Research Station field experiment (February 24, 2026) at this same site, covering four settings (two with a 16-species European stimulus set, two with a 30-species North American set) from six known speaker positions, one with a known hardware failure, with playback streams synchronized via PPS timing to about 1 cm in propagation distance and segmented into single-signal clips of 2.18-11.00 s (mean 5.07 s). Given TabPFN's in-context conditioning rather than training on all available data, I use an approximately 90/10 train-test split with the training set capped at 1,000 examples. I'm following the field-evaluation protocol: the model is trained on simulation only and evaluated on the real field recordings, with every field position withheld entirely from training, as well as evaluating on held-out simulation positions. My baseline, using just the hyperbolic solver's output (the point-estimate model input feature) before any gating or correction, gets the following on the frozen-lake site: on real playback recordings (Konnevesi), mean = 5.13 m, p50 = 0.41 m, p90 = 24.6 m, p95 = 42.1 m, p99 = 43.7 m; on simulation, mean = 0.17 m, p50 = 0.04 m, p90 = 0.21 m, p95 = 0.36 m, p99 = 3.88 m.

title: Adaptive Sequential Test Planning for Multi-Mechanism Reliability Qualification via Bayesian Monte Carlo Tree Search
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how the different pieces of the reward objective in my MCTS-SA planner contribute to avoiding catastrophic failures, and specifically wanted to isolate the effect of the safety barrier (proximity penalty) term. The mechanism is a barrier penalty that discourages the planner from approaching a state of catastrophic damage:
\begin{equation}
r_{\text{prox}} = -w_{\text{prox}} \cdot \left[\phi(D_{\text{EM}}) + \phi(D_{\text{TDDB}})\right]
\end{equation}
where $\phi(D) = \max(D - D_{\text{thr}}, 0)^{\gamma_{\text{barrier}}}$ with threshold $D_{\text{thr}} = 0.25$ and power $\gamma_{\text{barrier}} = 3$, weighted by $w_{\text{prox}} = 1200$.

title: Matryoshka Language Model Suites
prompt:
I've been ideating on how a Matryoshka-style nested training setup compares to just training independent models at matched compute. The core idea: instead of a conventional suite of $M$ models with $M$ independent parameter sets $\{(\theta_m, W_m)\}_{m=1}^M$, we enforce a strict nesting of parameters (aside from the LM head), $\theta_1 \subset \theta_2 \subset \cdots \subset \theta_M = \theta$, where each sub-model $T_{\theta_m}$ is its own Transformer stack with its own width $D_m$, depth $n_m$, and LM head $W_m$. One motivation is that classical suite training with distillation from the largest model into smaller ones normally requires either storing teacher logits offline or running the teacher in parallel, which adds compute or storage cost. In the Matryoshka setup, every forward pass through $\theta_M$ already produces logits for all $M$ sub-models at once, so online distillation from the largest to all smaller sub-models is essentially free. Concretely, I add a distillation term to each sub-model $m < M$, defined as the cross-entropy between teacher and student next-token distributions: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^{M \to m}_d = - \sum_{v=1}^{V} \texttt{stop\_grad}(\sigma(l^M_t)_v) \, \log \sigma(l^m_t)_v, \label{eq:distillation} \end{equation} where $\sigma$ is the softmax. The total loss for sub-model $m$ is a convex combination: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}^m = (1 - \alpha_d)\,\mathcal{L}^m_{\mathrm{ce}} + \alpha_d\,\mathcal{L}^{M \to m}_d, \label{eq:submodel-loss} \end{equation} and the overall training objective sums over sub-models: $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{L}^m$. The distillation coefficient $\alpha_d \in [0,1]$ controls the strength of the teacher signal.

My setup is a 3B Matryoshka suite with nested 500M/1.5B/3B sub-models, 39 total layers, with a depth triplet of 24/10/5, trained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu using the SmolLM2 tokenizer. The 500M and 1.5B Vanilla baselines mirror the SmolLM2 configurations at those sizes, and the 3B Vanilla baseline follows the Llama-3.2-3B shape. I've been brainstorming an idea around adding GFlowNet-based exploration plus an MLE stabilization stage on top of SFT for training an attack-generation model. I've been brainstorming around a setup where I evaluate LLM agents acting in a Supplier role against rational, non-LLM baseline policies, specifically looking at how a Supplier fares against an RE counterparty. RE here is approximated as non-engagement -- i.e. the counterparty either doesn't pay or doesn't deliver anything at all, so it's effectively a fully adversarial, immediately-defecting counterparty. title: Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
prompt:
I've been ideating on a retrieval-based correction mechanism for conformal prediction in time series, and I want to lay out the setup and where the baselines currently stand. The core idea is to split the interval construction into a retrieval stage and a correction stage. In the retrieval stage, each prediction context is encoded into a retrieval key z_t = psi_f(X_t, hat Y_t) before Y_t is observed, using whatever predictable forecaster features are available (input-window embedding, forecaster representation, point prediction features, exogenous variables, or their concatenation). Once a response at time i is observed, the key is appended to a knowledge base along with the realized one-sided residuals e_i^+ = (Y_i - hat Y_i)_+ and e_i^- = (hat Y_i - Y_i)_+, stored separately to allow different upper and lower tail behavior. Before time t, the knowledge base is K_{t-1} = {(z_i, e_i^+, e_i^-): i<t}, so the interval at time t only ever uses past residuals. Retrieval itself is done via KNN: N_K(t) = KNN_K(z_t, K_{t-1}, d), where d is instantiated as Euclidean distance, returning the K past indices closest to z_t. Retrieved residuals can be treated uniformly or weighted by distance, with weights w_i(t) = exp(-d(z_t,z_i)/tau) / sum_{j in N_K(t)} exp(-d(z_t,z_j)/tau) for i in N_K(t), where tau>0 controls concentration and uniform weights recover the hard top-K case. These weights define an empirical distribution used to compute local residual quantiles separately on each side: tilde R_t^+ = Q_{1-alpha/2}^{w_t}{e_i^+: i in N_K(t)} and tilde R_t^- = Q_{1-alpha/2}^{w_t}{e_i^-: i in N_K(t)}, giving the retrieved interval tilde C_t = [hat Y_t - tilde R_t^-, hat Y_t + tilde R_t^+]. Since this retrieved interval is locally adaptive but not calibration-certified (the retrieved set is finite and data-dependent, and quantiles can be unstable or biased when proximity in key space doesn't track future error behavior), I add a correction stage. For each calibration index j, once Y_j is revealed I compute B_j = max{ (Y_j - hat Y_j)_+ / tilde R_j^+, (hat Y_j - Y_j)_+ / tilde R_j^- }, a scalar nonconformity score normalized by the retrieved local scale rather than raw residual magnitude. Letting q = 1-alpha and q_n the finite-sample conformal quantile level, the correction is hat c = hat F_cal^{-1}(q_n) = Q_{1-alpha}({B_j : j in I_cal}), and the final interval is C_t^RCCP(hat c) = [hat Y_t - hat c * tilde R_t^-, hat Y_t + hat c * tilde R_t^+]. Values of hat c above one indicate the retrieved intervals tend to be too narrow on calibration data, while values below one indicate conservative retrieved intervals; direct retrieval corresponds to fixing this multiplier at one, whereas RCCP estimates it from the B_j distribution. For my setup, I'm comparing RCCP against split conformal prediction (SCP), online/adaptive methods EnbPI and SPCI, and localized methods NexCP, HopCPT, and ResCP. All methods use the same temporal partitions, frozen point forecasts, and random seeds, with hyperparameters selected on the calibration split when needed. I train a global LSTM forecaster on each dataset and evaluate at significance levels alpha=0.05 and alpha=0.15 (rather than the main alpha=0.1), averaging over multiple random seeds, to check whether behavior holds beyond the main setting. My baseline (SCP) results are as follows. title: SkillLens: Visual Skill Cards for Retrieval-Augmented GUI Action Prediction and On-Policy Distillation
prompt:
I've been developing a way to give a frozen computer-using agent a form of reusable visual procedural memory, rather than touching any model weights. The idea is that prior interaction experience gets converted (via a Trace-to-VSC process) into Visual Skill Cards that pair a procedure with state cues and visual evidence. At each decision step, the system ranks these cards against the current instruction and interface state, expands only the selected high-resolution evidence, and conditions the frozen executor on that evidence plus the live observation to predict the next GUI action.

A key design point is that retrieval and expansion are separated: cards are ranked first, and only the selected cards' evidence is expanded, since irrelevant VSCs can distract the executor and loading all card evidence for a single step is unnecessary. The default path is a lightweight, context-aware, site-aware text-indexed selector. Formally, the retrieval query at step $t$ is $q_t=Q(x,h_t,c_t)$, where $Q$ deterministically serializes the task instruction $x$, recent interaction history $h_t$, and selector-visible interface metadata $c_t$. For each card $s_i$, $d_i$ concatenates its identifier, name, goal, keywords, and available metadata; $\mathrm{Tok}(\cdot)$ returns the resulting token multiset, $\operatorname{supp}(\cdot)$ returns its unique-token support, and $n(u;r)$ counts token $u$ in record $r$. The shared support and coarse score are defined as \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\mathcal{U}_{t,i}&=\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(q_t))\cap\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(d_i)),\\ r_i^{(0)}(q_t)&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{t,i}}\min\!\left(n(u;q_t),n(u;d_i)\right)+b_i(c_t),\end{aligned}\end{equation} where $b_i(c_t)$ is a deterministic prior derived only from visible metadata (such as site or operation compatibility), and is zero when such metadata is unavailable. Coarse retrieval then produces \begin{equation}\mathcal{C}_t=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_c}(\mathcal{L};r_i^{(0)}).\end{equation} The default web path reranks only these candidates, using a compact candidate record $d_i^{\mathrm{cand}}$ containing the card identifier, name, goal, keywords, and visual tags: \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\mathcal{M}_{t,i}&=\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(q_t))\\&\quad\cap\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(d_i^{\mathrm{cand}})),\\ r_i^{(1)}(q_t)&=|\mathcal{M}_{t,i}|+0.1r_i^{(0)},\\ \widetilde{S}_t&=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_s}(\mathcal{C}_t;r_i^{(1)}),\\ \widehat{S}_t&=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_e}(\widetilde{S}_t;r_i^{(1)}),\\ S_t&=\{s_i\in\widehat{S}_t:\chi_i(c_t)=1\},\qquad E_t=\bigcup_{s_i\in S_t} e(s_i),\end{aligned}\end{equation} where $K_s$ is the selection budget, $K_e$ is the smaller expansion budget, $\chi_i(c_t)$ is an optional compatibility gate based only on visible metadata (defaulting to one), and $e(s_i)$ deterministically loads the bounded textual and visual evidence of card $s_i$. This closes the runtime path from the candidate set to the evidence actually consumed by the executor. A full-load strategy would pay \begin{equation}C_{\mathrm{full}} = \sum_{s_i\in\mathcal{L}} C(v_i),\end{equation} whereas this approach pays only the expansion cost for the selected evidence: \begin{equation}C_{\mathrm{lens}}(t)=C(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{C}_t)) + C(E_t).\end{equation} The board term is incurred only by board-based selector diagnostics and is zero for the default text-indexed selector. This cost expression captures the central design choice: retrieval decides where to look, and expansion controls how much visual evidence the executor sees.

My setup keeps the executor entirely frozen and changes only the runtime context, comparing No-skill against retrieved VSCs (with visual evidence expansion under the K_e/K_v budgets) across several frozen VLM executors: GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-4o, Gemini models, and Qwen3-VL-2B. I'm evaluating on Multimodal-Mind2Web (Step SR, Action F1, Element Acc.), WebLINX-BG (Overall, Intent Match, Element IoU), and OSWorld-G (Grounding Acc., bounding-box (BBox) Hit, Valid Output), with values reported as percentages.

My baseline (No-skill) results are: on Multimodal-Mind2Web, GPT-5.4-mini gets Step SR of 77.2% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Step SR of 4.6%; on WebLINX-BG, GPT-5.4-mini gets Overall of 12.8% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Overall of 14.1%; on OSWorld-G, GPT-5.4-mini gets Grounding Acc. of 45.0% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Grounding Acc. of 28.5%.

title: Path Integral Value Matching for Linear Quadratic Stochastic Optimal Control
prompt:
I've been working on a value-based approach to stochastic optimal control that I'm calling Path Integral Value Matching (PI-VM). The core idea builds on the observation that the path integral representation of the optimal value function has a recursive structure: for any $0 < t < s$, \begin{equation}\exp\left( - V(X_t, t) \right) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}^0}\Bigg[ \exp\left( - V(X_s, s) \right) \exp\left(- \int_{t}^{s} f(X_r,r)\,\mathrm{d}r \right) \, \Bigg | \, \mathcal{F}_t \Bigg], \quad V(x, 1) = g(x),\end{equation} where $X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the state of the uncontrolled stochastic process. This follows from the tower property of conditional expectation by decomposing the path integral into intervals $[t, s]$ and $[s, 1]$. The recursive structure suggests dynamic programming techniques can be adapted to solve for the value function iteratively, so I employ temporal-difference (TD) learning to approximate the recursive value dynamics, replacing high-variance long-horizon integration with stable short-term bootstrapping, and further integrate the Girsanov theorem with experience replay to enable off-policy training.

Concretely, my setup uses a Path Integral TD loss: for a state $x$ at time $t$, with a fixed lookahead horizon determined by $s = \min(1, t + M\Delta t)$, the loss is \begin{equation}\ell(\theta) = \left\| V_{\theta}(x,t) - \hat{V}_{\theta}(x, t, s) \right\|^2,\end{equation} where the target $\hat{V}_{\theta}$ is estimated via Monte Carlo approximation of the path integral using $N$ sample trajectories: \begin{equation}\hat{V}_{\theta}(x, t, s) = -\log \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N \exp\left( - \hat{\mathcal{W}}(X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}) - \hat{\mathcal{G}}(X^{(j)}_{s}) \right),\end{equation} where each trajectory $X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}$ follows the uncontrolled path measure $\mathbb{P}^0_{[t,s]}$ initialized at $X_t^{(j)} = x$, and \begin{equation}\hat{\mathcal{W}}(X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}) = \int_{t}^{s} f(X^{(j)}_r, r) \, \mathrm{d}r, \quad \hat{\mathcal{G}}(X^{(j)}_{s}) = \begin{cases} V_{\theta}(X^{(j)}_s, s) & s < 1, \\ g(X^{(j)}_s) & s = 1. \end{cases}\end{equation} This is distinct from a continuous limit of classical Bellman equations, and also distinct from risk-sensitive RL Bellman equations, since in my formulation the log-sum-exp applies to the optimal value function rather than to the value function itself.

For the experiments, I'm benchmarking on five tasks adapted from prior work: Linear Ornstein Uhlenbeck, Quadratic Ornstein Uhlenbeck (easy), Quadratic Ornstein Uhlenbeck (hard), Gaussian Mixture Models, and Many Well. The first three are unimodal SOC control problems, and I'm currently focused on those. I compare against several policy-based baselines, including relative entropy (RE), cross entropy (CE), variance (VAR), log-variance (LVAR), adjoint matching (AM), stochastic optimal control matching (SOCM), and stochastic optimal control matching with adjoint loss (SOCM-A). For the first three experiments I strictly align training hyperparameters with those used for SOCM. Across all experiments I use a 6-layer fully-connected neural network with GELU activations and the Adam optimizer. Since the ground truth optimal control is analytically tractable for these tasks, I use the control $\mathcal{L}_2$ Error as the primary metric: $\mathcal{L}_2 (u,u^*) := \frac{1}{d}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}^{u^*}} \left[ \int_0^1 \|u^* - u\|^2 (X^{u^*}_s, s) \, \mathrm{d}s \right]$, noting that this comparison is particularly stringent for my method since I infer the control indirectly via the gradient of the value function ($u = - \sigma^T\nabla V$), whereas the policy-based baselines optimize the policy directly. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU, with results averaged over four independent runs with distinct random seeds, and I also track training/inference timing per method.

For the adjoint matching (AM) baseline on the unimodal tasks, my current baseline results are: on OU Linear, control L2 error is 0.0 and time is 41.0ms; on OU Quadratic (easy), control L2 error is 0.00028 and time is 21.0ms; on OU Quadratic (hard), control L2 error is 0.00674 and time is 21.0ms.

My question about this setup: after switching from AM (my baseline above) to PI-VM (Ours), predict the resulting value for each: OU Linear Control L2 error; OU Linear Time (in ms); OU Quadratic (easy) Control L2 error; OU Quadratic (easy) Time (in ms); OU Quadratic (hard) Control L2 error; OU Quadratic (hard) Time (in ms).

Rather than asking a language model to forecast metrics, which was unreliable in my early tests, I rank candidates and execute only the one judged most promising, and in this variant the judge gets to run quick pilot experiments first, the way a researcher runs a small-scale check before launching a full experiment. The intervention is an Agentic RPM, which runs small-scale pilot experiments before choosing. A pilot experiment is a multi-turn interaction between a language-model agent and a sandbox that is an exact clone of the research agent's environment, including a single H200, the training data, the unlabeled test data and the pre-installed packages; the agent has python, bash and submit_solution tools, and submit_solution records a summary and analysis of the pilot findings rather than a selection. Because the agent tends to schedule its time too conservatively and to follow up only with hyperparameter tweaks, two mechanisms elicit more informative experiments: the prompt overstates the remaining time budget (the real budget is 300 s but the prompt reports 2700 s, 9 times larger), and after each submission a separate feedback model reviews the findings so far and either proposes the single most informative next experiment or signals that the evidence suffices, in which case the loop ends; the loop also ends when less than 60 s remain or after 30 pilot experiments. The pilot-experiment model and the feedback and final-prediction model share the same backbone without fine-tuning, and finally the candidate solutions, the task description and all submitted pilot findings go to the language model to pick the best candidate. At each child-creation step the chosen parent is mutated 15 times in parallel, and the Agentic RPM selects the single candidate to execute through pairwise comparisons in a tournament knockout, with up to K non-buggy previously evaluated nodes from the tree shown with their validation scores as context. To balance compute I deploy this selection only for the draft and improve operators and fall back to random selection during debug steps; the real pilot budget per step is 5 minutes, and that pilot time is spent inside the same 24-hour allocation as the research agent.

My setup is AIRA-dojo, an evolutionary tree-search scaffold that uses greedy parent selection (always mutating the node with the highest current validation score), a suite of mutation operators for distinct engineering phases (draft, improve and debug), and final selection of the node with the highest validation score across the tree. The benchmark is AIRS-Bench: 20 publicly released machine-learning research tasks under the text and tabular modalities, each specified by a problem, a dataset, a target metric and a published state-of-the-art value, with no baseline code. The agent gets a training dataset, test inputs and 24 hours on a single H200 per task, writes code that trains a model and produces a submission file, may run code that reports a validation score to guide its search, and never sees the hidden test score; the run is repeated for 10 seeds. Each task's test score is mapped to a Normalized Score through a log transform of the distance to the task's optimum, with NS = 0 at the worst score observed across all agents and NS = 1 at the public state of the art, and failed submissions scored 0; the reported number is the Average Normalized Score over tasks and seeds. To avoid the generalization gap that undermined long-horizon search in AIRA-dojo I use the Hidden Consistent Evaluation protocol. The child-creation operator and the RPM share a Qwen3.6-27B backbone, so any gain comes from the framework rather than a stronger selection model. In the No-RPM baseline the scaffold generates 15 candidate children at each operator step and picks one uniformly at random, which corresponds to vanilla AIRA-dojo in expectation. Two oracles that execute all 15 candidates at each step and keep the highest scorer (only the selected candidate's compute counts towards the 24 hours) bound what greedy child selection can achieve: the validation oracle reaches 0.748 and the test oracle, which uses privileged test-set information, 0.759.

My baseline is the No-RPM scaffold. Its final Average Normalized Score after the full 24-hour allocation is 0.684, and by construction it needs the whole 24 hours to reach that score.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been ideating on a windowed forgetting mechanism for the state-level rollout statistics in the graph-structured difficulty estimator. Right now, the online inference procedure accumulates rollout feedback across training steps by inheriting the state-level Beta posterior, i.e. \(a_{k,t}^{\mathrm{hist}}=a_{k,t-1}\) and \(b_{k,t}^{\mathrm{hist}}=b_{k,t-1}\). The concern motivating this is that the rollout distribution is non-stationary since the policy parameters keep changing during RL optimization, so rollout observations collected many training steps earlier may no longer accurately characterize the success probability of the current policy. The windowed mechanism I'm considering keeps the difficulty-aware sample graph \(W\), the smoothed assignment prior \(A\), the Potts graph prior, and the mean-field variational family from the main method unchanged, and only changes how historical rollout evidence is organized: state-level success probabilities would be estimated from a recent sliding window, while the complete rollout history of each previously observed sample is still retained for sample-level prediction. Concretely, instead of directly inheriting the complete Beta posterior from the previous step, the windowed variant reconstructs the state-level Beta parameters from a fixed prior and the rollout evidence within the current window: \begin{align} a_{k,t}^{(L)}=a_0+S_{k,t}^{(L)},\qquad b_{k,t}^{(L)}=b_0+F_{k,t}^{(L)}. \end{align} In my implementation, I set \(a_0=b_0=1\), corresponding to the uniform prior \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\), which is a standard weak prior for a Bernoulli success probability that doesn't favor any particular success rate before rollout evidence is observed, and it guarantees the Beta parameters stay strictly positive -- important since under a finite window some latent states may get no rollout observations in the current window. When \(S_{k,t}^{(L)}=F_{k,t}^{(L)}=0\), the \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) prior still yields a valid posterior and keeps the posterior mean and the digamma terms used in the variational updates well-defined and numerically stable. Ideally the prior mean \begin{align} \mathbb{E}[\theta_{k,t}]=\frac{a_0}{a_0+b_0} \end{align} should be close to the average success probability of the current policy, which would give a more informative default for latent states with few or no recent observations, but getting a reliable estimate of that would require evaluating a sufficiently large and representative subset of the training set at each stage, adding substantial rollout cost, and estimating it only from scheduler-selected samples would be potentially biased since those samples aren't representative of the full training distribution -- so I adopted \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) as a practical trade-off among prior neutrality, numerical stability, and computational efficiency. The posterior mean success probability of latent state \(k\) is then \begin{align} \mu_{k,t}^{(L)}=\frac{a_{k,t}^{(L)}}{a_{k,t}^{(L)}+b_{k,t}^{(L)}}. \end{align} The model-based prediction for sample \(x_i\) retains the same mixture form as in the main method: \begin{align} \widehat{p}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{model}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{ik,t}\mu_{k,t}^{(L)}. \end{align} When the window covers all preceding training steps, this windowed formulation reduces to the cumulative-history variant; with a finite \(L\), rollout observations older than \(L\) training steps no longer directly contribute to the current state-level success probabilities. My setup is to evaluate this windowed variant by replaying the full training logs of Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the GRPO training runs for the graph-structured difficulty estimator, and compare against the cumulative estimator used in the main experiments, looking at sample-level MAE and the correlation metric \(r\) on the MATH training split for both models. My baseline gets: on the MATH training split with Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B, the cumulative estimator (Ours) has MAE = 0.183 and r = 0.836; on the MATH training split with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the cumulative estimator (Ours) has MAE = 0.131 and r = 0.776.

My question about this setup: after switching from Ours (cumulative estimator) (my baseline above) to Windows (windowed variant), predict the resulting value for each: MATH training split (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) MAE; MATH training split (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) r; MATH training split (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) MAE; MATH training split (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) r.

title: The Role of Grid Cells in Reducing Spatial Aliasing in Hippocampal Place Representations
prompt:
I've been working on integrating grid cells into a place cell representation to see how they interact with boundary vector cell (BVC) inputs when disambiguating spatially similar locations. The core idea is that place cells integrate two input streams: BVCs provide geometric constraints from environmental boundaries, while grid cells (GCs) contribute metric phase information that can disambiguate perceptually similar locations. The relative contribution of these two streams is controlled by a weighting parameter η ∈ [0,1], where BVC inputs are weighted by (1-η) and GC inputs by η.

My setup uses an analytical grid cell and BVC-driven place cell model with 8 head-direction cells, 400 BVCs, grid cells divided into 8 modules of 50 cells each (400 grid cells total, spatial scale λ=5.5, giving an activation diameter of roughly 2.7m), and 1000 place cells, trained via competitive Oja-rule learning while the agent explores. The agent is a Roomba-like bot in Webots with a compass for head-direction updates and a rangefinder with 720 beams covering 360 degrees (max range 25m) feeding into the BVC layer, and all environments used are 20m x 20m in size. For the open environment, 5 trials were run for each configuration (with and without grid cells), with training continuing until 95 percent coverage was reached (0.5m bin size) and evaluation continuing until 99 percent coverage was reached (0.2m bin size, matching the bin size used for the Mean Spatial Aliasing Index, MSAI, metric). In the no grid cell condition, η is set to 0 so that BVC inputs alone drive the place cell layer.

My baseline in the open environment with no GC (η=0, BVC-only) gets an MSAI of 5.7×10⁻⁴.

title: Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training
prompt:
I've been working on an idea around attested-subject content injection — basically manipulating truth/attestation status of an injected subject rather than fluency or form, and seeing whether that distinction shows up in downstream training dynamics. The two fluent passages we compare are matched in register and structure, both 194 tokens long, and differ only in whether the subject is corpus-attested (Jimmie Nicol, who appears 4 times in the training corpus) or fabricated (Gizmo Harrington, who appears zero times, counts taken before any run existed). The attested subject is also the one whose passage happens to be true, so anything a contrast between the two picks up can't be pinned on attestation alone, since truth rides along with it. Fluent-attested/fluent-fabricated names how the passages were constructed, and the model-side variable the contrast manipulates is whether the subject is attested in the training corpus.

My setup is 32 GPT-2 (124M parameter) models trained from scratch on OpenWebText, split into 4 conditions x 8 seeds. Each model is trained from an initialization of random weights (dictated by the seed), using a corpus of 2,499,805,184 training tokens and 10,485,760 held-out tokens, both from OpenWebText. There are 9,536 total steps in each pre-training run, with warmup of 200 steps so learning rate first reaches its 6e-4 peak at step 200. I inject at peak learning rate deliberately, defined as the maximum update-step size. The injection replaces one row of a 256-row batch outright at step 200, using a fixed 1024-token context (identical across arms and seeds) carrying the 194-token passage at position 400. Because the injected row replaces a whole row, an arm and its twin differ across the entire row while two arms differ only in the 194-token span — which is why the passage-specific analyses contrast two arms against each other rather than an arm against its twin. The row's slot within the batch is derived from the seed (75, 191, 229, 129, 19, 44, 192, 93), while the row's contents are not, so all across-seed spread comes from the models rather than the stimulus.

We matched full-batch gradient delta (the quantity that actually reaches the optimizer when the row is swapped) as the target across fluent arms: 0.010698 for fluent-fabricated and 0.010683 for fluent-attested, a 0.14\%\ difference. Sequence-level norm (the row's own gradient strength) is reported alongside but wasn't the matching target: 2.1521 vs 2.1496, a 0.11\%\ difference. random-chars sits at 0.011788 with cosine 0.790 relative to the other two arms, marking it as a different kind of perturbation moving in a variant direction. Measured against the seed-matched twin at the injected step, the change in full-batch gradient norm is +0.00049, +0.00063, and +0.00050 for fluent-fabricated, fluent-attested, and random-chars respectively, against a twin norm of 0.518 — about 0.1\%\ for all three arms, much smaller than the 2.2\%\ figure from the matching table, since that table reports the norm of the gradient difference, which is largely orthogonal to the batch gradient.

My primary registered variable is interpolation loss barrier: I take the finished weights of a run and its seed-matched twin, walk the straight line between them at 21 evenly spaced points, evaluate held-out cross-entropy at each, and calculate the barrier as the maximum departure from the chord between the two endpoint losses. The held-out section is text carved out before training that no model ever saw, and neither subject appears in it, so the measurement is blind to the manipulation. I use 512 held-out windows, each a 1024-token strip taken as the contiguous non-overlapping prefix of the held-out split. My registered secondary variable is held-out cross-entropy itself. Each condition's displacement is measured from its seed-matched twin on both variables at the final checkpoints; the two fluent conditions are each differenced from their own twin first, then those differences are differenced against each other within seed. One confirmatory comparison was registered (fluent-fabricated minus fluent-attested on interpolation loss barrier), so no multiple-comparison correction applies.

My baseline currently gets, for the fluent-attested (corpus-attested subject) arm measured against its seed-matched twin, an interpolation loss barrier (mean displacement from twin over the 8 seeds) of 0.1462 barrier units.

I've been mulling over how to make zero-shot counters actually respect the category they're told to count, rather than just detecting all salient objects regardless of label. The idea I keep coming back to is image-guided exemplars: instead of specifying a category through text, the data engine specifies it from one real reference image, synthesizing a visual support set—a gallery of target exemplars alongside galleries of its distractors—and then categorizing each localized point by matching it against these galleries. At inference, given a target category, its support set, and a test image, the frozen counter proposes a set of candidate points, one per detected object, and the task is to decide which of them belong to the target. Following the projection step, I pool and project each candidate into an embedding $P_\theta(f_p)$, and reduce the support set to a positive gallery $\mathcal{G}^+$ of target prototypes and a negative gallery $\mathcal{G}^-$ of distractor prototypes (one prototype per exemplar). A candidate is accepted when it more closely resembles the target than any distractor: \begin{equation}\mathrm{accept}(p) = \big[\, s^+(p) > s^-(p) \,\big], \qquad s^+(p) = \max_{g \in \mathcal{G}^+} \langle P_\theta(f_p), P_\theta(g)\rangle, \quad s^-(p) = \max_{g \in \mathcal{G}^-} \langle P_\theta(f_p), P_\theta(g)\rangle,\end{equation} and the predicted count is the number of accepted candidates. This is a nearest-exemplar rule: the single closest prototype across both galleries decides each candidate's label, with no per-category threshold to tune. Specifying a new target only swaps $\mathcal{G}^+$ and $\mathcal{G}^-$, leaving the counter, the backbone, and $P_\theta$ untouched. My setup is to evaluate this on the PrACo benchmark, which measures whether a model adheres to the specified category—a known failure mode for many zero-shot counters. I'm specifically looking at the Negative Test protocol, which prompts each image with every candidate category and reports NMN (the mean count predicted for absent categories normalized by the ground-truth count of the present one) and PCCN (the percentage of images whose present-category count is closer to ground truth than its absent-category counts; higher is better). My baseline gets, for CountGD++ (Text⊕⊖ +pseudo) on the PrACo Negative Test: NMN = 0.07 and PCCN = 97.99%.

My question about this setup: after switching from CountGD++ (Text⊕⊖ +pseudo) (my baseline above) to CountGD + RECOUNT (Image⊕⊖), predict the resulting value for each: PrACo (Negative Test) NMN; PrACo (Negative Test) PCCN (in %).

title: Context as an Environment: Programmatic Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents
prompt:
I've been ideating on how long-horizon LLM agents manage their accumulated interaction history, and specifically whether it makes sense to keep serializing that history into the model's prompt at all versus treating it as an external environment the model interacts with programmatically. The idea I'm working through, Scroll, realizes the session state as a Session Environment with three parts: an append-only Event Log that is the durable, ground-truth record of an agent's sessions (every interaction appends a typed event with role, session and agent identifiers, timestamps, and tool state, receiving an immutable, monotonically increasing seq, stored in SQLite, with BM25 as the default search since it's deterministic and needs no index-time model calls); durable storage for payloads, where small payloads stay inline in SQLite and large ones move to JSON or artifact storage on the filesystem with the row keeping a bounded preview and a recovery pointer, accessed via lazy handles (ToolResultRef, ArtifactRef); and a persistent runtime with a resident namespace, where a sandboxed Python kernel persists across model calls throughout the session and holds environment objects (resident Python values and lazy handles with type, size, and provenance metadata tied to the events they derive from), with the harness prepending a namespace digest to every call listing each resident variable's name, type, and shape (small scalars shown inline), and model-authored code running in a fail-closed sandbox where the Event Log is read-only from the kernel and database/filesystem/network/tool access is limited to harness-declared capabilities. The prompt itself only carries a working view rather than the full serialized history. My setup compares four agents that all share the same backbone (Qwen3.8-Max) and toolset on the LOCA benchmark, differing only in how they manage a growing context: a summarization agent (a ReAct agent that periodically compacts its interaction history into a summary), a retrieval agent (a ReAct agent whose overflowing history is evicted and made accessible through a recall tool), a CodeAct agent that interacts with the environment through programmatic tool calling, and Scroll. The harness and evaluation protocol are held fixed across all four, varying only the context-management strategy, and I'm looking at performance at 128K and 256K environment description lengths. My baseline currently is the summarization agent: on LOCA_128K it gets 86.7% accuracy, on LOCA_256K it gets 65.3% accuracy, which is an absolute drop from 128K to 256K of -21.4Δ.

My question about this setup: after switching from Summarization Agent (my baseline above) to Scroll (ours), predict the resulting value for each: LOCA_128K accuracy (in %); LOCA_256K accuracy (in %); LOCA absolute drop from 128K to 256K (in Δ).

title: SSE-Bio: A Structured Self-Evolving Agent with Agentic Retrieval Policy for Multi-Hop Biomedical Reasoning
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to fairly account for the inference cost of the full SSE-Bio agent relative to the strongest prior self-evolving and agentic baselines, Biomni and STELLA, especially since SSE-Bio incorporates a local Proxy module alongside the Manager, Dev, Critic, and retrieval components. The Proxy is responsible for explicitly controlling whether external knowledge should be introduced at each reasoning round: at reasoning round $t$, it selects a retrieval action $a_t \sim \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid u_t)$, with $a_t \in \mathcal{A} = 2^{\{\mathrm{KG},\mathrm{TPL}\}}$, where $\mathrm{KG}$ and $\mathrm{TPL}$ denote knowledge-triplet retrieval and template retrieval respectively, yielding four possible actions (retrieving neither source, only knowledge triplets, only templates, or both). When $\mathrm{KG}\in a_t$, SSE-Bio uses the information gap field in $u_t$ as the retrieval query, encodes it together with candidate biomedical triplets using BiCA, and returns the top-$K$ triplets after schema and duplicate filtering; when $\mathrm{TPL}\in a_t$, it uses the task type encoded in $u_t$ as the retrieval query, applies the same BiCA-based retrieval procedure to the long-term memory $\mathcal{E}$, and returns the top-$K$ compatible template. My setup is to evaluate on the BioHopR test split and measure end-to-end per-example inference cost for each agent system, including all Manager, Dev, Critic, retrieval, and local Proxy operations, with the local Proxy adding no commercial API calls but its latency still included in the end-to-end measurement. title: Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basins in Autoresearch Agents
prompt:
I've been thinking about why independent autoresearch runs on the same task end up at such different scores. In my harness an agent repeatedly edits a solver, runs it and submits for a score, and runs that share the same initial state and model still plateau for long stretches at different levels, with gaps that persist after a lot of extra compute. Mapping the submitted artifacts by functional similarity suggests each run stays in a localized region of the solution space, an idea basin, and spends its remaining budget refining there. Committing the whole budget to one run is pure exploitation, while best-of-N (N independent runs of budget B/N, keep the best) is pure exploration that leaves N minus 1 accumulated workspaces wasted. I want an interpolation that uses the variance across runs to help an ongoing run escape its basin. The intervention is fork-and-flush, which alternates parallel sampling with serial execution on a fixed schedule. Forking creates K parallel agents that each inherit the current lineage and get an exploration budget; when that budget is spent, the highest-scoring branch is kept and the others are discarded, so the selection chooses between basins rather than refining within one. Flushing keeps the accumulated workspace but empties the conversational context, because a branch that kept the chat history would carry the parent's reasoning and tend to re-enter the same basin. A run opens with K = 4 agents launched from empty workspaces and keeps the best as the leader; the leader continues alone until 33% of the budget is consumed, when K = 4 new branches fork from its workspace with empty chat contexts, each with an exploration budget of about 0.06B, and the best branch becomes the new leader; the same happens at 66%, and the final result is the best score found by any agent in the run. The schedule is fixed rather than plateau-triggered, since a stall clock rarely fired in development runs and its tolerance is hard to tune across tasks.

My harness runs GitHub Copilot CLI (version 1.0.73) against an isolated container. Execution is a sequence of submission episodes: within an episode the agent edits its solver, runs it and submits for a score as often as it chooses; an episode ends when the agent halts itself or hits a token budget, and the harness then resumes the agent with a short continuation prompt. Across episodes both the workspace (the files it has produced) and the conversational context (its chat history) are preserved, and interventions happen only at episode boundaries. A deterministic grader scores the workspace, a run's result is the best score found by any lineage it instantiated, and budgets are metered in credits, a fixed function of model tokens (100 credits is about US$1). The tasks are polyomino (pack a given set of polyominoes into a bounding rectangle of minimal area, C++ heuristic; scored as a ratio to a reference solution; 25k credits per run), job-shop (order operations on machines to minimize the makespan; ratio to known bounds; 10k credits), AHC014 (a port of AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014; ratio to a reference; 10k credits), p150 and p171 (ports of two other AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems; ratio to a reference; 10k credits each), sphere-pack (pack equal spheres in a cube; normalized between a grid baseline and the Kepler bound; 6k), relay-lay (K-hub facility location with up to 2 x 10^5 clients; a cost-ratio score, unclipped above the baseline; 6k), LWE-rec (recover the secret of 200 structured-LWE instances drawn from ten families of graded difficulty; number of instances solved; 6k), LLM-SQL (reorder the rows and columns of an LLM-over-SQL workload to maximize the prefix KV-cache hit rate; rescaled hit rate where 100 is perfect; 6k), order-add (black-box permutation optimization over 1000 elements against a cost oracle; official judge score, at most 100; 6k), Borden-inv (recover a 3D groundwater contaminant source from well readings, with the agent writing both the forward model and the inverter; tier-gated judge score; 10k credits), kernel (Anthropic's performance-engineering take-home, optimizing a kernel for a simulated VLIW machine whose deterministic simulator counts cycles; simulated-cycle score, higher is better; 100k), and tinyCIFAR (train a CIFAR classifier that trades test accuracy against compressed model size; merit in (0,1), an accuracy gate times a log-size term read on a sealed test split; 31k). Budgets were set per task to where single runs plateau, and single runs last from several hours to several days. Within a task every condition uses the same model, GPT-5.6-terra at high reasoning effort for eleven tasks and GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort for kernel and tinyCIFAR, with the same tools, prompt and task workspace. I run eight independent single-run baselines per task and five runs of each other condition (four on tinyCIFAR), and report the mean final score per task on the task's own scale.

My baseline is the single-run agent, one lineage spending the full budget sequentially, averaged over eight independent runs per task. Its mean final scores are: polyomino 88.56; job-shop 9.66; AHC014 23.71; p150 123.47; p171 84.26; sphere-pack 43.87; relay-lay 72.59; LWE-rec 155.3; LLM-SQL 26.9; order-add 24.6; Borden-inv 64.62; kernel 120.36; tinyCIFAR 0.429.

title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
prompt:
I've been iterating on how to keep a group of autoresearch agents from stalling. Given a problem, each agent proposes a candidate, a judge evaluates it, and the agent uses the scores and feedback to decide what to try next; the search state records every candidate with its score and feedback, and the session holds the messages and reasoning that produced them. My hypothesis is that an agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts as this history grows, making fewer and smaller edits, and that simply running agents in parallel does not escape this because each one still carries its own growing session. The idea I'm testing combines two changes. First, communication: a team of agents works on the same problem in parallel, each in its own session and with its own search state, and before each proposal every agent gets access to the other agents' candidates as commits along with their scores; there is no point-to-point messaging, so communication is asynchronous and token-free. Second, forgetting: the search is divided into rounds, and at the end of each round every agent discards its session together with the search state and keeps only the best candidate found so far along with its score; a new agent then starts the next round from this candidate with an empty context and the same instructions as the first round. For a team, every agent restarts from the single best candidate across the team. The rationale is that the best candidate already contains most of the progress, while the discarded state mainly records how that progress was made, and the new agent is no longer conditioned on earlier failed attempts. My team has four agents and forgets three times, which splits its budget into four rounds; the total money spent equals that of the baseline.

My harness runs each agent in a loop: a reducer decides which candidates the agent sees as files in its workspace and which session it continues, the agent edits a candidate using only file tools, a judge scores the result, and the harness records the new candidate as a commit in a version-controlled repository together with the judge's score and feedback. Every configuration I compare is a setting of that reducer. Every agent is a Pi agent with its default system prompt, running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the prompts describe the task and the loop and give the agent no strategy for the search itself. The four tasks are AHC014, a C++ heuristic solver for AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014 (on a grid with initial dots, repeatedly add a dot that completes a rectangle with three existing dots; maximize the mean score over 30 official test cases, where dots far from the center count more; I report the score in thousands), the VLIW kernel from the Anthropic kernel performance challenge (a Python kernel for a simulated VLIW SIMD machine that traverses a tree and hashes a batch of values; minimize clock cycles, which start at 147,734 for the reference implementation), Frontier-CS Q171 (a C++ program that, on a 20 x 20 grid, visits 40 target squares in a given order by moving, sliding until blocked, and placing or removing blocks, using as few actions as possible; maximize the mean score over 75 test cases, scaled per case from 0 for a greedy baseline to 100 for a reference solution), and nanochat-autoresearch (a PyTorch script that trains a small language model for 5 minutes on one H100; minimize validation bits per byte). The money budget per replicate is $20 for AHC014, $40 for the VLIW kernel, $20 for Q171 and $20 for nanochat, identical across configurations, and I run each configuration three times per task and report the best final score and the mean of the three final best scores.

My baseline is four parallel agents that split the budget without seeing one another's work and continue their own sessions throughout. On AHC014 their best run ends at 1007 (thousand) and the three runs average 964 (s.d. 57). On the VLIW kernel the best is 1172 cycles and the mean 1220 (s.d. 44). On Frontier-CS Q171 the best is 71.4 and the mean 70.2 (s.d. 1.1). On nanochat-autoresearch the best is 0.979 BPB and the mean 0.980 (s.d. 0.001).

title: Runtime Control for AI Agents: Closing the Evaluation--Execution Gap in Operational Workflows
prompt:
I’ve been developing a state-bound temporal re-evaluation approach — essentially a runtime control layer that tracks decision dependencies and re-adjudicates before dispatch, rather than carrying a one-time allowance forward. The idea is to compare a point-in-time evaluation configuration that adjudicates a proposal once and never rechecks validity against a state-bound configuration that uses the same recorded policy, authority, and signal inputs, plus a whole-state fingerprinting ablation that treats all case-state changes as relevant. title: MiCLA: Mixture-to-Constituent Latent Alignment for Polyphonic Audio Representation Learning
prompt:

title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation
prompt:
I've been iterating on a hallucination-aware code translation approach I'm calling HaluCodeTran, and I'm comparing it against a standard Retrieval Augmentation (RA) baseline. The idea is to integrate retrieval-augmented translation with a feedback loop that prompts the model to examine its intermediate outputs against the source logic and a hallucination taxonomy. The process has three primary phases: 1) Knowledge Augmentation, 2) Code Translation, and 3) Recursive Self-Reflection.

For Knowledge Augmentation, given an input source code $x$, I use a knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ of high-quality source–target pairs and apply the BM25 algorithm to retrieve a subset of relevant examples $\mathcal{S}$ based on lexical and structural relevance to $x$. These examples provide implicit knowledge about target-language syntax, library usage, and idiomatic patterns.

In the Code Translation phase, the model generates an initial translation candidate $\hat{y}^0$ conditioned on $x$ and $\mathcal{S}$:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{y}^0 = \text{Translate}(x, \mathcal{S})
\end{equation}

Then the Recursive Self-Reflection loop begins. At each iteration $i$, the model receives the source program $x$, the current translation $\hat{y}^i$, the retrieved examples $\mathcal{S}$, and the taxonomy definitions. It produces a reflection report $\mathcal{R}^i$ that checks whether $\hat{y}^i$ preserves source-program behavior, uses valid target-language syntax and APIs, and avoids project-context deviations. This reflection step does not observe hidden test results; it relies only on the source code, retrieved examples, and taxonomy-guided inspection. If $\text{IsConsistent}(\mathcal{R}^i)$ returns true, the process terminates. Otherwise, the model distills a structured critique $\mathcal{T}^i$ from the report, where each critique item follows the format \lstinline|<category: location: description: repair hint>|, with \lstinline|category| being one of the hallucination subtypes, \lstinline|location| identifying the suspicious target-code fragment, \lstinline|description| explaining the mismatch, and \lstinline|repair hint| stating the required source-aligned revision. The refinement step is:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{y}^{i+1} = \text{Refine}(\hat{y}^i, \mathcal{T}^i, x)
\end{equation}
This cycle iterates until no hallucination is detected or a maximum step $M$ is reached. The same $M$, retrieval size, and prompting budget are used across models in the mitigation study.

My evaluation setting uses the CodeNet dataset, which provides balanced language-pair coverage and executable test cases for all six translation directions (C++↔Java, C++↔Python, Java↔Python). For each model, I construct a retrieval database from source programs and their successfully translated target programs in the model's successful pool. The evaluation set contains the remaining source programs that were not successfully translated by the same model under the vanilla setting. During retrieval, the query program itself is excluded from the candidate pool, and the model receives only retrieved source–target examples rather than test outputs or reference explanations. title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
prompt:
I've been mulling over how to handle cases where validation metrics don't meet the performance thresholds we set during planning. The idea is to trigger a parallel hyperparameter optimization step inside MedicalMLOmni to refine the configuration. My setup is this: when validation metrics $m$ fail to meet the thresholds $\tau$ extracted during planning, MedicalMLOmni spawns $n$ HPO agents that independently explore hyperparameter modification strategies. Each agent receives the current plan $\pi$, the validation metrics $m$, and the execution logs as input. Each HPO agent constructs literature search queries by prompting the LLM to combine underperforming metric names, current hyperparameter values from $\mathcal{H}$, and task properties, submitting them to the search APIs used during planning. The agents are prompted to focus on different hyperparameter categories—optimization adjustments, regularization strategies, or architecture-specific parameters—to ensure diverse exploration. Retrieved results undergo extraction to identify adjustment strategies reported for similar tasks, and each agent scores them based on relevance to the observed performance gap. Each agent then generates a candidate configuration $\mathcal{H}'_i$ along with a confidence $C_i \in [0,1]$ reflecting cross-source consistency and task alignment, and an uncertainty $U_i \in [0,1]$ quantifying search quality and hyperparameter variance across sources. MedicalMLOmni aggregates the candidates $\{\mathcal{H}'_1, \mathcal{H}'_2, \ldots, \mathcal{H}'_n\}$ with weights $w_i = C_i / (1 + U_i)$, prompting the LLM to synthesize a refined configuration $\mathcal{H}^*$ by selecting consensus hyperparameters, resolving conflicts through weighted voting, and combining complementary adjustments. This updates the plan to $\pi' = (\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}, \mathcal{H}^*)$, which re-enters execution for retraining. For high-uncertainty scenarios where $\max_i(U_i) > 0.7$, MedicalMLOmni can optionally present candidate configurations with their confidence and uncertainty scores to users for validation before retraining. The parallel HPO process iterates until $m$ satisfies $\tau$ or the maximum iterations are reached. title: Fragment-Level Graph Encoding for Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about moving from atom-level to fragment-level graph encoding for molecular property prediction, specifically using a BRICS decomposition to define the fragments. The idea is to see whether a coarser graph representation can serve as a useful inductive bias, particularly in data-sparse settings. My setup is as follows. Each molecule is decomposed with BRICS as implemented in RDKit, which makes the decomposition deterministic. Given atom feature vectors \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{34}\), the fragment node feature is the element-wise sum over the atoms assigned to fragment \(f\):

\begin{equation}
  h_f = \sum_{i \in f} x_i,
  \label{eq:sum}
\end{equation}

The procedure is: (1) find BRICS-cleavable bonds, (2) break them without adding dummy atoms, (3) map each atom to its resulting fragment, (4) sum atom features per fragment as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:sum}, (5) add an undirected edge between two fragments for each cleaved bond, and (6) give every fragment–fragment edge the same constant scalar attribute, so that no bond-type information enters.

I am evaluating this on the PTR1 regression dataset. Unlike BACE and BBBP, PTR1 has no curated public benchmark. 250 compounds were manually compiled from sixteen primary medicinal-chemistry resources published between 2009 and 2022. We include PTR1 as a representative of the data situation in an early-stage program against a neglected-disease target: a few hundred literature measurements rather than a benchmark with little prospect of obtaining more. The evaluation is correspondingly small. Scaffold splitting over 119 Bemis–Murcko scaffolds, 82 of them singletons, sends every multi-member scaffold group to training and leaves 25 molecules each for validation and test. Because of this, model selection is unreliable, as can be expected in a data-sparse early-stage program.

title: Investigating the Impact of Learner Errors on Social Bias in Large Language Models
prompt:
I've been iterating on a setup where learner errors are injected into prompts to see how they affect model behavior. The idea is to simulate L2 writing by introducing four error types simultaneously into the input, and my default configuration uses the gender category because gender is the only demographic axis shared across all three benchmarks I'm working with, which lets me compare trends across them. Since the four error types co-occur in real L2 writing, this setting makes the evaluation closer to a realistic scenario.

My setup uses five open-weight models from three families: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. I'm measuring accuracy on tasks whose correct answer is not tied to a stereotype, to rule out the objection that any accuracy loss merely reflects a general degradation of comprehension. Specifically, I'm using MMLU, which contains no demographic content, and the disambiguated split of BBQ, where the context states the correct answer. My baseline with clean prompts (0% error rate) gets the following: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 68.8%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 95.7%, race 96.3%, religion 93.1%; Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 82.5%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 100.0%, race 99.6%, religion 98.8%; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 75.2%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 98.6%, race 98.4%, religion 94.6%; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 79.0%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 98.8%, race 97.7%, religion 97.0%; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 82.8%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 100.0%, race 100.0%, religion 98.2%.

title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
prompt:
I've been iterating on isolating the contribution of typed role tokens in my formatting-aware parsing approach. The novel component of this system is not preserving cues—docx2python does that—but attaching typed roles to them. Isolating that contribution requires comparing our representation against the same representation with the role tokens removed and every inline cue marker retained. My setup is the upper panel: all six arms, 76 documents, 3 repeats, 1,368 calls, paired per-document macro F1 against ours. The pre-registered confirmatory test of the typing claim runs once on 79 documents with 6 repeats (1,422 calls) and three arms only, so the correction family is two hypotheses. Both arms in H1 show the model identical inline cue markers over byte-identical content, differing only in whether a typed role token is attached. On the 76 real policy documents for marked-requirement set retrieval, my baseline with untyped markup gets micro F1 of 0.605, precision of 0.811 proportion, and a false positive rate of 0.01.

My question about this setup: after switching from ours, untyped markup (my baseline above) to ours (formatting-aware, typed roles), predict the resulting value for each: 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement set retrieval) micro F1 (in F1); 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement set retrieval) precision (in proportion); 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement set retrieval) FP rate (in rate).

title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
prompt:
I’ve been thinking about domain-invariant training, specifically using an adversarial domain classifier (DANN). The idea is to encourage representations that do not depend on the domain during training, adversarially, using the source identifier as the domain label. My setup is a ResNet18 backbone whose first convolution takes five input channels. I train with standard empirical risk minimization on the training sources and apply the classifier to the test sources unchanged. My baseline gets: overall test set accuracy 0.175, POSCON subset accuracy 0.465, TARGET subset accuracy 0.012, REST subset accuracy 0.002.

My question about this setup: after switching from ResNet18 (no adaptation) (my baseline above) to DANN, predict the resulting value for each: Overall test set accuracy (in fraction); POSCON subset accuracy (in fraction); TARGET subset accuracy (in fraction); REST subset accuracy (in fraction).
